a: On the road he has brought my strength low;
t: "My strength" or "his strength"; the Greek hears an answer
p: The Hebrew is written "his strength" but read "my strength." The Greek reads the verb as "answered."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the reading aloud (Qere)
readings.en: he afflicted my strength on the way
readings.plain: On the road he has brought my strength low;

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the written form (Ketiv)
readings.en: he afflicted (me) on the way (with) his strength
readings.plain: With his strength he has brought me low on the road;

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.orig: ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ ἐν ὁδῷ ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ
readings.en: he answered him in the way of his strength
readings.plain: He answered him on the road of his strength:

why: The read form fits the lament: the sufferer's own strength is broken halfway through life, as the next lines say. The written form "his strength" is possible (God humbled him by his strength), and the Greek also read "his," but it took the consonants of "afflicted" as "answered" and so turned the verse into a dialogue.
b: In the Greek the next words become the speaker's request: "Tell me how few my days are" (see the next variant). Some Church Fathers read the whole passage as the Father answering the Son. Hebrew 102:24.

a: he has made my days short.
t: "He has made my days short" or "Tell me how few my days are"
p: The Greek reads the same consonants as a request: "Tell me the fewness of my days."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: he has shortened my days
readings.plain: he has made my days short.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.orig: τὴν ὀλιγότητα τῶν ἡμερῶν μου ἀνάγγειλόν μοι
readings.en: the fewness of my days declare to me
readings.plain: tell me how few my days are.

why: The Hebrew makes good sense as a complaint and leads directly into the plea of 102:24. The Greek follows from its reading of the first line as "he answered him" and needs a different word division and vowels.
b: Compare Psalm 39:4: "LORD, show me my end, / how many days I am measured out," where the request is in the Hebrew itself. Hebrew 102:24.

a: Long ago you set the earth on its foundations;
p: The Greek adds "Lord" (kyrie) to this verse, and Hebrews 1:10 quotes it with that word.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: long ago you founded the earth
readings.plain: Long ago you set the earth on its foundations;

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees); quoted in Hebrews 1:10
readings.orig: κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς σύ, κύριε, τὴν γῆν ἐθεμελίωσας
readings.en: in the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth
readings.plain: In the beginning, Lord, you set the earth on its foundations;

why: No Hebrew manuscript known to this site has "LORD" here. The Greek may have supplied it to make the address clear; some point to "my God" in 102:24, others to free translation.
b: This small addition matters for Hebrews 1:10–12, which reads the verse as spoken to the Son: "You, Lord, in the beginning" (a fresh rendering). With the word "Lord" the address is explicit. See the chapter page. Hebrew 102:26.

a: you will change them like clothing, and they will be gone.
p: Vaticanus reads "roll them up," the form in Hebrews 1:12. The main Greek text has "change."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: like clothing you change them, and they pass away
readings.plain: you will change them like clothing, and they will be gone.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text, with most manuscripts)
readings.orig: καὶ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον ἀλλάξεις αὐτούς, καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται
readings.en: and like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed
readings.plain: you will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (as printed by Tischendorf) and a few other Greek copies; the form quoted in Hebrews 1:12
readings.orig: καὶ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον ἑλίξεις αὐτούς, καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται
readings.en: and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed
readings.plain: you will roll them up like a cloak, and they will be changed.

why: The Hebrew plays on one verb, chalaf, used twice: you change them, and they change (pass away). The main Greek text agrees, with "change" (allaxeis). The Greek is divided: Vaticanus and a few copies read "roll up" (helixeis), as Hebrews 1:12 does. Scholars debate whether those copies were brought into line with Hebrews, or whether Hebrews used such a copy; Isaiah 34:4, where the heavens are rolled up like a scroll, may lie behind the image.
b: Hebrews 1:12 follows the Greek, and in the best manuscripts of Hebrews adds a second "like a garment" (hōs himation), which the later Byzantine text of Hebrews lacks. Hebrew 102:27.

a: He fills your years with good things,
p: The Hebrew word 'edyekh is unclear. The Greek reads "your desire."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); the vowels give 'edyekh, a word usually meaning "ornament"
readings.en: who satisfies with good your (ornament? years? life?)
readings.plain: He fills your years with good things,

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.orig: τὸν ἐμπιπλῶντα ἐν ἀγαθοῖς τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν σου
readings.en: who fills your desire with good things
readings.plain: He fills your desire with good things,

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew consonants and takes them, with many modern scholars, as "your duration, your years" (from 'ad, "lasting"), which suits "you grow young again." Elsewhere the word means "ornament" (Exodus 33:4), which makes little sense here; the KJV guessed "thy mouth." The Greek "desire" may be a guess from context.
b: Other proposals are "your being" or "your life" (by comparison with Psalm 32:9, another hard place with the same word). No Dead Sea copy examined for this page differs here.

a: he keeps in mind that we are dust.
p: The Hebrew says "he is mindful"; the Greek turns it into a prayer: "Remember that we are dust."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: remembering that dust we are
readings.plain: he keeps in mind that we are dust.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees); some Greek copies read "he remembered"
readings.en: remember that we are dust
readings.plain: remember that we are dust.

why: The Hebrew participle fits the hymn, which speaks about God in the third person. The Greek imperative likely reads the same consonants with different vowels (zekhor, "remember!").
b: Tischendorf's apparatus notes that some witnesses read the past tense, emnēsthē, "he remembered."

a: He makes the winds into his messengers
p: A Dead Sea copy reads singular "messenger" and "servant." The Greek reads "angels" and "spirits."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) and Greek ("making his angels spirits, and his servants a flame of fire")
readings.en: making his messengers winds (or: the winds his messengers)
readings.plain: He makes the winds into his messengers

readings.w: 4QPs-l (4Q93), a Dead Sea scroll, as reported by The Dead Sea Scrolls Bible
readings.en: making his messenger a wind
readings.plain: He makes the wind into his messenger

why: The Masoretic plurals are supported by the Greek. The scroll's singulars are reported in a published translation and may be a scribal simplification.
b: The Greek angelous ... pneumata, "his angels spirits," is the form quoted in Hebrews 1:7; see the note on this verse.

a: The deep was the robe you put over it;
p: The Greek reads "The deep is like a garment, his covering," taking the deep as God's robe.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the deep, like a garment, you covered it
readings.plain: The deep was the robe you put over it;

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.orig: ἄβυσσος ὡς ἱμάτιον τὸ περιβόλαιον αὐτοῦ
readings.en: the deep, like a garment, is his covering
readings.plain: The deep, like a robe, is his covering;

why: The Hebrew "you covered it" (the earth, 104:5) fits the next line, in which the waters stand above the mountains. The Greek read the consonants as a noun, kesuto, "his covering," perhaps influenced by 104:2, where light is God's robe.
b: The Hebrew agrees with Genesis 1:2, where the deep covers the earth before the waters are gathered.

a: the pine trees are the stork's house.
t: "The stork's house in the pines" or "the heron's house leads them"
p: The Greek reads "the heron's house leads them," from a reading "at their head" for "pine trees."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: the stork, the junipers (or pines) are her house
readings.plain: the pine trees are the stork's house.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.orig: τοῦ ἐρωδιοῦ ἡ οἰκία ἡγεῖται αὐτῶν
readings.en: the heron's house leads them
readings.plain: the heron's house leads them.

why: The Hebrew beroshim, "junipers" or "pines," fits the trees of 104:16. The Greek read the same consonants as berosham, "at their head," which gives a strange sense.
b: Ancient Christian readers built allegories on the Greek line, with the heron's nest as the head of the household of the birds.

a: Praise the LORD!
p: The Hebrew ends Psalm 104 with "Praise the LORD!" The Greek makes it the title of the next psalm.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: praise Yah
readings.plain: Praise the LORD!

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees) (Alleluia as the title of Greek Psalm 104, Hebrew 105)
readings.en: Alleluia (heading the next psalm)
readings.plain: (Alleluia begins Psalm 105)

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew verse division. The Greek treats "Alleluia" as a heading, as it does at the start of Psalms 105, 106 and 107 (Greek 104–106). The Talmud also notices that this is the first "Hallelujah" in the Psalter (Bavli Berakhot 9b–10a).
b: The same question arises at 105:45 and 106:1: the Hebrew ends 105 and begins and ends 106 with the word, while the Greek has it as a title over 105, 106 and 107.

a: you seed of Abraham, his servant,
p: The Greek and a Dead Sea scroll read "his servants." 1 Chronicles 16:13 reads "seed of Israel."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: seed of Abraham, his servant
readings.plain: you seed of Abraham, his servant,

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees); 11QPs-a, as reported by The Dead Sea Scrolls Bible
readings.en: seed of Abraham, his servants
readings.plain: you seed of Abraham, his servants,

readings.w: 1 Chronicles 16:13, Masoretic Text
readings.en: seed of Israel, his servant
readings.plain: you seed of Israel, his servant,

why: Abraham is "his servant" again at 105:42, so the singular is likely original. The plural makes the line match the plural "his chosen ones" in the next line, which is the kind of change copyists make.
b: 11QPs-a is also reported to read "his chosen one," singular, in the second line. The Chronicles form makes both lines name Jacob (Israel).

a: They tormented his foot with fetters;
p: The Hebrew is written "his feet" but read "his foot."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the reading aloud (Qere)
readings.en: they afflicted with the fetter his foot
readings.plain: They tormented his foot with fetters;

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the written form (Ketiv); also the Greek
readings.en: his feet
readings.plain: They tormented his feet with fetters;

why: The site follows the read form at Ketiv and Qere places. The difference makes no change to the sense.
b: The Greek "his feet" (tous podas autou) agrees with the written form.

a: to tie up his officials as he wished
p: The Greek reads "to instruct his officials as himself," from a Hebrew verb one letter different.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: to bind his officials at his will
readings.plain: to tie up his officials as he wished

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees); also the Syriac, as reported by Allen and Kraus
readings.orig: τοῦ παιδεῦσαι τοὺς ἄρχοντας αὐτοῦ ὡς ἑαυτόν
readings.en: to instruct his officials as himself
readings.plain: to instruct his officials to be like himself

why: "To bind" makes a pointed contrast with 105:18, where Joseph himself was bound. The Greek read leyasser, "to discipline, instruct," which fits the second line, "to make his elders wise." Both readings are old, and many modern scholars prefer the Greek here.
b: The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. The Greek "as himself" reads kenafsho for benafsho, a common confusion of two similar letters.

a: They set out his signs among them
p: The Hebrew says Moses and Aaron "set out" the signs. The Greek and the Syriac make God the subject.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: they set among them the matters of his signs
readings.plain: They set out his signs among them

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs); the Syriac agrees, as reported by Allen
readings.orig: ἔθετο ἐν αὐτοῖς τοὺς λόγους τῶν σημείων αὐτοῦ
readings.en: he set among them the words of his signs
readings.plain: He set out his signs among them

why: The plural fits 105:26, which has just named Moses and Aaron, and Exodus, where they stretch out the staff and their hands (Exodus 7:19–20). The singular makes the line match the rest of the plague list, where God acts (105:28–36), and so may be a smoothing.
b: Either way the signs are "his," God's. The Hebrew "matters (or words) of his signs" is an idiom for the signs themselves.

a: and they did not defy his word.
p: The Hebrew says "they did not defy his word." The Greek leaves out "not."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the reading aloud (Qere)
readings.en: and they did not rebel against his word
readings.plain: and they did not defy his word.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the written form (Ketiv)
readings.en: his words
readings.plain: and they did not defy his words.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.en: and they embittered (provoked) his words
readings.plain: and they defied his words.

why: The Hebrew is harder and so more likely original: a scribe would sooner drop a puzzling "not" than add one. Without it, the line refers to the Egyptians' resistance; with it, the subject is Moses and Aaron, or the plagues (see the note).
b: Some scholars emend the verb to shameru, "they did not keep," with the Egyptians as subject. No manuscript has this.

a: LORD, keep me in mind with the goodwill you show your people;
t: "Keep me in mind" or "keep us in mind"
p: The Greek reads "remember us" and "visit us," making the whole psalm speak as "we."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: remember me, LORD, with the favor of your people
readings.plain: LORD, keep me in mind with the goodwill you show your people;

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.orig: μνήσθητι ἡμῶν, κύριε, ἐν τῇ εὐδοκίᾳ τοῦ λαοῦ σου
readings.en: remember us, Lord, with the favor of your people
readings.plain: LORD, keep us in mind with the goodwill you show your people;

why: The singular is the harder reading in a psalm that otherwise says "we," and the Greek probably smoothed it. The singular "I" continues in 106:5 in the Hebrew.
b: The Greek also has "visit us" in the second line.

a: and they were defiant at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds.
t: "At the sea" or "as they went up"
p: The Greek reads "as they went up at the Red Sea." Some scholars propose "against the Most High."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and they rebelled at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds
readings.plain: and they were defiant at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.orig: καὶ παρεπίκραναν ἀναβαίνοντες ἐν τῇ ἐρυθρᾷ θαλάσσῃ
readings.en: and they provoked as they went up at the Red Sea
readings.plain: and they were defiant as they went up, at the Red Sea.

readings.w: A modern conjecture, no manuscript (compare Psalm 78:17; Psalm 78:56)
readings.en: and they rebelled against the Most High at the Sea of Reeds
readings.plain: and they were defiant against the Most High at the Sea of Reeds.

why: The Hebrew repetition "at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds" is awkward but intelligible. The Greek read 'olim, "going up," for 'al-yam. The conjecture 'elyon matches Psalm 78:17, "defying the Most High in the parched land," and Psalm 78:56, but has no manuscript support.
b: The Greek always names the sea "the Red Sea"; see the topic on the Sea of Reeds.

a: but he sent a thinning sickness down their throats.
p: The Hebrew says God sent "leanness"; the Greek says he sent "fullness" into their souls.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and he sent leanness into their throat
readings.plain: but he sent a thinning sickness down their throats.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐξαπέστειλεν πλησμονὴν εἰς τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν
readings.en: and he sent fullness into their souls
readings.plain: but he sent fullness into their souls.

why: The Hebrew fits Numbers 11:33, where a plague struck while the meat was still in their mouths. The Greek may have read mazon, "food," for razon, or may simply have followed Numbers 11:20, where the meat comes "until it comes out of your nostrils."
b: The KJV's "leanness into their soul" follows the Hebrew; see the note.

a: They traded their glory
p: Scribal tradition lists this verse among places where "my glory" was changed to "their glory" out of reverence.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and they exchanged their glory
readings.plain: They traded their glory

readings.w: Tiqqune soferim, a rabbinic list of scribal "corrections" (Mekhilta and later Masoretic notes); no manuscript
readings.en: my glory (God speaking)
readings.plain: They traded my glory

readings.w: Some Greek manuscripts, as noted in Tischendorf's apparatus (most Greek copies agree with the Hebrew)
readings.en: his glory
readings.plain: They traded his glory

why: All Hebrew manuscripts read "their glory," and it makes good sense: God was Israel's glory (Jeremiah 2:11). The tradition of scribal correction says the text once read "my glory" and was changed to avoid saying that God himself was exchanged; scholars differ on whether such lists record real changes.
b: Romans 1:23, "they traded the glory of the God who does not decay" (a fresh rendering), may echo a form of this verse that named God's glory.

a: and their children too, among the nations,
p: The Hebrew repeats "make fall" from the previous verse. Many scholars restore "scatter," as in Ezekiel 20:23.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and to make their seed fall among the nations
readings.plain: and their children too, among the nations,

readings.w: A modern conjecture, no manuscript (compare Ezekiel 20:23)
readings.en: and to scatter their seed among the nations
readings.plain: and to scatter their children among the nations,

why: The Hebrew can be read as continuing 106:26: God swore to make the fathers fall in the wilderness, and their children among the nations. The conjecture lehafits differs by one letter and matches Ezekiel 20:23 exactly, so it is attractive, but the Greek agrees with the Hebrew.
b: Either way, the psalm reads the exile back into the oath of the wilderness; see the note on 106:26.

a: But Phinehas rose and gave judgment,
p: The Greek says Phinehas "made atonement," taking the word from Numbers 25:13.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and Phinehas stood and judged (intervened)
readings.plain: But Phinehas rose and gave judgment,

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.en: and Phinehas stood and made atonement
readings.plain: But Phinehas stood up and made atonement,

why: This is a matter of translation more than of a different text: the Greek translator interpreted vayfallel from Numbers 25:13. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew word's usual sense, "judge, arbitrate."
b: The Aramaic Targum reads "he prayed," as reported by Stec's translation.

a: and changed his mind, so many were his acts of loyal love.
t: "His acts of loyal love" or "his loyal love"
p: The Hebrew is written "his loyal love" (singular) but read "his acts of loyal love" (plural).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the reading aloud (Qere)
readings.en: according to the abundance of his loyal loves
readings.plain: and changed his mind, so many were his acts of loyal love.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), the written form (Ketiv)
readings.en: according to the abundance of his loyal love
readings.plain: and changed his mind, so great was his loyal love.

why: The site follows the read form at Ketiv and Qere places. The plural matches 106:7, "your many acts of loyal love."
b: The Greek has "according to the abundance of his mercy" (kata to plēthos tou eleous autou), singular, in agreement with the written form.

a: And let all the people say, "Amen!"
t: "Amen" or "So be it, so be it"; a command or a report
p: The Greek translates Amen as "So be it, so be it." Chronicles turns the command into a report.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: and let all the people say, Amen
readings.plain: And let all the people say, "Amen!"

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint, Rahlfs' critical text; Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Tischendorf, agrees)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐρεῖ πᾶς ὁ λαός· γένοιτο γένοιτο
readings.en: and all the people will say: So be it, so be it
readings.plain: And all the people will say, "So be it, so be it!"

readings.w: 1 Chronicles 16:36, Masoretic Text
readings.en: and all the people said, Amen
readings.plain: And the whole people said, "Amen!"

why: The Psalm's own Hebrew is followed. The Greek translates Amen as it does at the ends of Books I to III. Chronicles narrates the people's answer and adds "and gave praise to the LORD" in place of "Praise the LORD!"
b: This is one reason many scholars think Chronicles knew the Psalter with Book IV already closed by this doxology.
